column3: You are a local administrator. From a non-elevated token, bypass UAC to get a full-integrity SYSTEM-capable shell.

column3: Domain administrator - full control of the Active Directory domain.
Can back up and restore any file (SeBackup/SeRestore) - read SAM/SYSTEM or write a SYSTEM binary.
Can manage services on domain controllers - reconfigure a service binary to run as SYSTEM.
Can load printer drivers (SeLoadDriver) - a route to kernel code execution.
Can manage most domain accounts (not admins) - a strong AD foothold.
Can load an arbitrary DLL into the DNS service, which runs as SYSTEM on a DC.
column4: dnscmd to load a malicious DLL

column3: Full control of VMs - effectively host-level access.
column4: abuse VM management for host access

column3: Can log in over RDP. Not privilege on its own, but useful access.
Can use WinRM (PowerShell Remoting) to this host.
Can launch/activate DCOM objects - some lead to lateral movement or local escalation.
Read the event logs - recon, and sometimes credentials logged in plaintext.
Can create/edit GPOs - a powerful AD escalation if linked to privileged OUs.
The literal Administrator account name appearing in a groups/users list - note, not itself a group membership.
The standard Users group. Normal, non-privileged.
Everyone. Normal; only interesting when it appears in a permissive ACL.
